title: Oracle patches 1295 security vulnerabilities in October, including six scoring 10.0
raw_text: Oracle has patched 1295 security vulnerabilities with its October Critical Patch Update Advisory ; six of them scored the highest vulnerability rating of 10.0 on the CVSS version 3.1 scale. The company’s flagship Oracle E-Business Suite was home to one of the vulnerabiltiies, tracked as CVE-2026-101809 . This enables any unauthenticated attacker with network access via HTTP to compromise the workflow notification mailer in the suite’s Workflow component, taking over Workflow and potentially affecting other products too. The flaw affects Workflow versions 12.2.3 through 12.2.15. Oracle SOA Suite, part of Oracle Fusion Middleware, was hit by three of the bugs rated 10.0. One, tracked as CVE-2026-91231 , is in the Adapters component, and enables unauthenticated attackers to compromise Oracle SOA Suite resulting in its takeover, with potential impact on connected products. Two others were in the Fabric Layer component of Oracle SOA Suite: CVE-2026-91216 and CVE-2026-91221 . Both are easily exploitable, Oracle said, and enable an unauthenticated attacker with network access via the T3 or IIOP protocols to compromise Oracle SOA Suite and perhaps affect other products too. The bugs appear in supported versions 12.2.1.4.0 and 14.1.2.0.0. There’s a 10.0-rated vulnerability in another part of Oracle Fusion Middleware too. The flaw in Oracle Access Manager (tracked as CVE-2026-87337 leaves it open to compromise by any unauthenticated attacker with network access via HTTP. Successful attacks of this vulnerability can result in unauthorized creation, deletion or modification of critical data on Oracle Access Manager versions 12.2.1.4.0 and 14.1.2.1.0. The last “perfect 10” vulnerability in Oracle’s latest report is in the JD Edwards EnterpriseOne Orchestrator product of Oracle JD Edwards, tracked as CVE-2026-91299 . This enables an unauthenticated attacker with network access via HTTP to compromise and take over versions 9.2.0.0 through 9.2.26.5 of the orchestrator. This article first appeared on CIO .

title: Dual BIOS: The laptop security feature SMBs don’t know they need
raw_text: Every security checklist starts with the basics: strong passwords, multifactor authentication, spotting phishing, and keeping software up to date. All four protect what happens after a laptop starts. But some attackers are more focused on what happens before. That’s the domain of the BIOS, the first code that runs when a laptop powers on. It checks the hardware, then hands control to the operating system. Malware planted at this level can load before the operating system does, so it can evade antivirus tools and even survive a drive wipe or reinstall. For small and midsize businesses (SMBs), the cost of an incident goes beyond the bill to fix it. It’s also about the work that stops in the meantime. The Verizon Business 2026 Breach Impact Study (which analyzes cyber insurance claims), found that SMBs suffered losses accounting for up to 7% of their total revenue. It also identified business interruption as the fastest growing source of loss. Detection isn’t recovery Modern laptops verify their firmware before booting, so a tampered BIOS image usually fails, though attackers are increasingly exploiting flaws that enable them to slip past those checks. But even a failed attack can do damage, because a BIOS that doesn’t pass verification can leave the laptop unable to boot. Of course, not every BIOS failure is malicious. An update that’s interrupted, such as a laptop losing power before it finishes, gives the same result. Either way, a corrupted BIOS effectively bricks the device. IT must spend time and money restoring or replacing it, and in the meantime, a remote employee can lose days of work waiting for a replacement. What’s more, if the failure was the result of a cyberattack, the business may need to reset credentials and possibly notify customers. How a dual BIOS provides a second chance The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) frames firmware security around 3 goals: protect firmware from unauthorized changes, detect unauthorized changes, and recover quickly and securely. Recovery is the part that keeps employees working. Some laptop manufacturers are now providing SMBs with an effective defense against compromised or corrupted firmware. A dual BIOS, sometimes called a dual ROM design, puts two firmware chips on the motherboard. The first holds the system BIOS, while the second stores a protected copy. In this way, if the primary BIOS becomes corrupted, the laptop can fail over to the backup, and employees can get back to work almost immediately. That’s because recovery doesn’t require a network connection or a call to the help desk. Firmware resilience for small teams Dual BIOS designs have long been common in servers, where staying available is critical, as well as in gaming PCs and higher-end enterprise machines, but few small businesses think to look for this capability. However, with so many employees working remotely and with attackers increasingly targeting firmware, a dual BIOS is rapidly becoming a necessary security capability for an SMB laptop. The ASUS ExpertBook A7 brings dual BIOS protection to small-business laptops. If the laptop detects a BIOS integrity failure during startup, recovery begins automatically. The event is also recorded in the BIOS System Event Log, so IT can confirm what happened, and the log can flag signs of physical tampering, such as the laptop’s case being opened. The ExpertBook A7 is also powered by up to an Intel ® Core™ 7 Series 3 processor to keep multitasking, communication, browsing, and content creation moving smoothly throughout the workday. SMB laptops don’t need to be vulnerable to firmware attacks or corruption. A dual BIOS deserves a place on every SMB’s list of required laptop features. Learn more about the ASUS ExpertBook A7.

All four protect what happens after a laptop starts. But some attackers are more focused on what happens before. That’s the domain of the BIOS, the first code that runs when a laptop powers on.

title: Meta hit with $25 billion fine for illegally sharing user data
raw_text: A judge in New Mexico has fined Meta $25 billion for its flouting of data privacy laws between 2010 and 2021, including its controversial passing of data to Cambridge Analytica . The action serves as a stark reminder to enterprises not to play fast and loose with data protection legislation, as the consequences could be highly damaging. Meta faced the court action after it was revealed that data company Cambridge Analytica had improperly obtained personal data that Facebook was holding. It could have been even worse for Meta. Under New Mexico law, the damages could have been as high as $219 billion , which would have exceeded its revenue for 2025. Judge Francis Mathew reduced his demand to $25 billion without explanation, but was scathing in his judgment on the social media company. “The harm in this matter is difficult to overstate, and goes to the heart of Facebook’s basic business proposition,” he wrote in his order . The company had committed more than 43 million violations of New Mexico’s consumer protection laws and had deceived its users by giving third-party app developers access to personal information without consent. The company is set to appeal against the judgment. It’s been a bad couple of months for Meta. In August, the company agreed to an $18 billion settlement over claims that Facebook and Instagram failed to prevent children from accessing its platforms. And in July, another judge in New Mexico fined the company just under $1 billion for, again, failing to protect minors. In Europe, companies are also under pressure over data protection. Last year, breaches of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) rose 22% , with a record €1.2 billion in fines issued, as legislators look to get tougher on big tech companies. This article first appeared on Computerworld .
